hook.line: Tomás finds a photo of a young man in Rosa's album and shows it to everyone at the café. Spanish puts a tiny *a* in front of a person you know, look for or visit.
hook.en: Don Hernando, do you know this man? (formal)

examples.en: Do you know my brother? (to a friend)

examples.es: Visito a mis papás los domingos.
examples.en: I visit my parents on Sundays.

rule:
When the verb lands on a specific person, Spanish puts *a* in front of them. English has nothing there, so just leave it untranslated:
*Conozco a Vale.* I know Vale.
*Visito a mi abuela.* I visit my grandmother.

Things and places don't get it: *Conozco Medellín. Busco el baño.*

Two cases skip it even with people. After *tener*: *Tengo dos hermanas*. And when it's any person, not a particular one: *Busco un mesero* (any waiter will do).

Remember *a* plus *el* makes *al*: *Busco al señor Gómez*.
smallPrint: Teachers call this the personal *a* (*a personal*).

yourTurn.prompt: Fill the gap and type the whole sentence: Visito ___ mi abuela. (a / nothing)
yourTurn.why: Your grandmother is a specific person, so she gets *a*.

yourTurn.prompt: Fill the gap and type the whole sentence: Tengo ___ dos hermanos. (a / nothing)
Do you know Mariana? (to a friend)
yourTurn.why: Mariana is a specific person: *a Mariana*.

yourTurn.prompt: I know Medellín, but I don't know your family. (to a friend)
yourTurn.answer: Conozco Medellín, pero no conozco a tu familia.
yourTurn.why: A city gets no *a*; people you mean do.

yourTurn.prompt: Swap the thing for a person: Busco el café. Now you're looking for Vale.
yourTurn.why: A thing takes no *a*; a person does.

yourTurn.prompt: Make it about Hernando: Vale llama a su hermana. (Hernando calls his grandchildren.)
yourTurn.why: Grandchildren are people, so the *a* stays.

pitfalls.why: Almost. Vale is a person, so Spanish wants *a* in front.
*Tener* is the exception: no *a*, even for people.
Cities and things don't get the *a*; only people do.
